# What’s the Fed’s next move? 

September 25, 2026

 The Fed raised rates in September, marking the first hike in three years. Is this the start of a longer hiking cycle? 

 

## Key takeaways

- The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) concluded its September meeting by voting unanimously to raise rates by a quarter point, bringing the federal funds rate to 3.75–4.0%.
- The hike came amid persistent inflation concerns, with core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation running above 3% every month of 2026, as well as “geopolitical developments,” according to the FOMC statement.
- J.P. Morgan Global Research forecasts another quarter-point raise in December, but does not expect a longer-term hiking cycle.

## Why did the Fed hike rates in September?

The FOMC voted unanimously to raise rates by a quarter of a percentage point, to 3.75–4.0%, at the conclusion of its September meeting, in line with market expectations.

# The Fed raised rates for the first time since 2023, and its officials now see 4.1% through 2027 — a full point above their March path

 Maxwell Milan· Sep 24 · 3 min read 

- The FOMC raised the federal funds target range by a quarter point to 3.75%–4% on 16 September, by 12 votes to none — its first increase since July 2023, after six cuts totalling 1.75 points.
- The median projection for the funds rate at the end of 2026 has gone from 3.4% in March to 3.8% in June and 4.1% now, implying one more quarter-point rise this year.
- For the end of 2027 the median moved from 3.1% in March to 3.6% in June and 4.1% now — the median official no longer expects a cut next year.
- Projected 2026 PCE inflation was raised from 2.7% in March to 3.7%; the latest actual reading, for July, is 3.7%.
- The 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.01% on 16 and 18 September, its highest close since July 2007.

# Fed’s Barr says future interest rate hikes ‘likely’ needed to tame inflation 

 by Max Rego - 09/23/26 7:12 PM ET 

 by Max Rego - 09/23/26 7:12 PM ET 

Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr said Wednesday the central bank will “likely” raise interest rates again to counter persistent inflation, after it did so last week for the first time in three-plus years.

Barr, a member of the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), said the unanimous decision to raise the benchmark interest rate by a quarter point was the “right” one, given that inflation “is above our 2 percent target and not clearly trending toward target in a timely way.”

The Fed governor added, “In my base case, further policy adjustments are likely to be needed to ensure inflation comes down to target in a timely fashion,” during a housing affordability summit hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago.
